Louis Sullivan. The American architect and theorist who pioneered the modern skyscraper and championed ornamental design in industrial architecture, coining the maxim that form follows function.

Sullivan lived from 1856 to 1924. He designed the Wainwright Building in St. Louis in 1891, one of the first skyscrapers to express vertical structure as aesthetic principle, establishing the template for American tall buildings. He created the Guaranty Building in Buffalo in 1896, featuring a terracotta facade with flowing organic ornament, demonstrating how industrial buildings could achieve beauty.

Sullivan coined the phrase form follows function, rejecting historical revival and arguing that building design must emerge from its purpose. This principle became the guiding maxim of modernism. He designed ornamental systems incorporating Art Nouveau influence, flowing naturalistic patterns integrated into terra cotta, metalwork, and carved detail.

Sullivan founded the Chicago School with his partner Dankmar Adler, developing the steel-frame skyscraper while rejecting the historical pastiche of eastern architects. He mentored Frank Lloyd Wright as a draftsman, profoundly influencing Wright's approach to organic design and structural honesty. Sullivan wrote extensively on architecture, including Kindergarten Chats and A System of Architectural Ornament, developing the theoretical foundations of modernism.

His ornamental language drew from and influenced Art Nouveau, though he applied these flowing forms to steel and terra cotta in industrial contexts. Frank Lloyd Wright was his direct apprentice and absorbed Sullivan's philosophy of integrating form with nature and function. Sullivan was the founder of the Chicago School, the movement that developed the modern skyscraper and transformed American cities through innovative use of steel-frame construction.
